speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: Chairman, I seek to move, "That the sum to be allocated for Head J of the Estimates be reduced by $100".

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: Within which, Dr Ng described the changing international order in the decades post-World War II, and how the United States (US) and the leading western powers reconstructed, rebuilt and redefined the international system after the war.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: The most important product of it all was a rules-based system to promulgate an international order for shared interest and mutual benefit.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: While we have the same players and largely the same rules today, the rules based system and the alliances that formed post-World War II appears to be under threat.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: This marks a rift between US and its European North Atlantic Treaty Organization (NATO) allies.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: We have yet to see the full impact of the new US administration's trade, economic and foreign policies, and what this means for international institutions and alliances, as well as for the US' role and presence here in the Asia Pacific.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: China continues to grow as a power, both economically and militarily.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: Closer to home, China continues its military exercises in the South China Sea and along the Taiwan Straits, areas that remain perennial sources of tension.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: Most recently, it conducted live firing naval exercises circumnavigating Australia, which has caused consternation for the Australians.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: Globally, the two major conflicts continue to simmer.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: While there is a ceasefire in the Isreal-Hamas conflict at the moment, this appears tenuous, with both sides making allegations against the other for not having honoured the terms to ceasefire.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: Against this backdrop, where collective security and the rules-based order appear to be fraying, the Ministry of Defence (MINDEF) and the Singapore Armed Forces (SAF) will be important for Singapore's safety and security.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: I would be grateful if the Minister can share, what is MINDEF's evaluation of the security situation in the world and the region, and its approach to the potential threats Singapore may face.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: Mr Chairman, in recent years, the global geopolitical environment has been plagued with uncertainty, heightened tensions and a clear weakening of international order.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: It has now been three years since Russia's invasion of Ukraine, in what was a clear and flagrant violation of sovereignty and territorial integrity.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: The war continues to escalate with ongoing clashes in the physical and cyber domain.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: On the physical battlefield, Russia has occupied large swathes of Ukraine's eastern regions and is continuing its advance, with no end in sight.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: The cyber battlefield has also seen its shares of issues, with multiple attacks on critically important Ukrainian infrastructure since the start of the conflict.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: Nothing has been spared from this cyber warfare, from disinformation campaigns powered by artificial intelligence (AI) and deepfakes, to cyberattacks on Ukrainian governmental websites to missile strikes on Ukrainian data centres.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: And yet, amidst the backdrop of the Russia-Ukraine war, is also the devastating Israel-Hamas conflict.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: While temporary ceasefire has been agreed in January this year, allowing both sides to exchange hostages, the final outcome is still shrouded in uncertainty.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: This brief reprieve does not undo the months of conflict that have taken a catastrophic humanitarian toll, deepened global divisions and polarise countries along political, religious and ideological lines, to the detriment of social cohesion and harmony between the global citizenries.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: The conflict has also caused wider impact throughout the Middle East, drawing countries such as Iran, Lebanon and Yemen into the disarray.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: Both conflicts have demonstrated how the nature of warfare continues to evolve.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: There have been significant advancements in emerging technologies, both in terms of conventional high-end capabilities, as well as low cost and dual-use technologies.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: The world is now a far more dangerous and uncertain place.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: To some, these conflicts may seem distant and far from our shores.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: Considering these recent developments in external security environment, can MINDEF share an update on its plans and priorities to strengthen the SAF, in line with SAF2040.

speaker: Mr Shawn Huang Wei Zhong (Jurong)
text: At last year's Committee of Supply (COS) debate, the Minister for Defence said that a sustained defence spending was the most efficient and effective means of building a strong military over the long term.

speaker: Mr Shawn Huang Wei Zhong (Jurong)
text: We cannot wait until conflict is at our doorstep before we upgrade our capabilities to defend ourselves.

speaker: Mr Shawn Huang Wei Zhong (Jurong)
text: The SAF must continually build robust military capabilities to counter escalating threats in our increasingly volatile world.

speaker: Mr Shawn Huang Wei Zhong (Jurong)
text: Ongoing conflicts around the world show the uncertainty of our times.

speaker: Mr Shawn Huang Wei Zhong (Jurong)
text: In particular, the war in Ukraine highlights the vulnerability of smaller states and how we need to be prepared.

speaker: Mr Shawn Huang Wei Zhong (Jurong)
text: Asian countries have also been increasing their military capabilities and spending.

speaker: Mr Shawn Huang Wei Zhong (Jurong)
text: Such spending patterns are testament to our troubled times.

speaker: Mr Shawn Huang Wei Zhong (Jurong)
text: It is clear that defence remains a large and important area of investments in many parts of the world, and the SAF should similarly keep pace.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair
text: Chairman, Singapore is a digital nation, with robust digital infrastructure and with people accessing a wide range of services through digital means, including communications, Government services, banking and ecommerce.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair
text: As both we and the world become increasingly interconnected and reliant on digital technology, we would also have new vulnerabilities that adversaries can exploit if we are not careful.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair
text: On the military front, cyberattacks can disrupt military command and control systems, intelligence and surveillance operations, even the functionality of weapons systems.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair
text: In fact, the low cost of entry for cyber operations means anyone can engage in cyber warfare.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair
text: Unlike traditional military domains, where power is often correlated with economic resources and industrial capacity, the digital domain has very low barriers for entry.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair
text: Determining the source of the attack can also be difficult and may hinder our responses, making it even more crucial for the military to develop sophisticated strategies to deal with them.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair
text: The pace of technological change in the digital domain is rapid and relentless.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair
text: The military must continuously adapt to emerging technologies to stay ahead on our defence.

speaker: Mr Neil Parekh Nimil Rajnikant (Nominated Member)
text: Mr Chairman, Sir, cyber threats pose a significant risk to the security and economic stability of nations, especially for a global hub like Singapore.

speaker: Mr Neil Parekh Nimil Rajnikant (Nominated Member)
text: We are vulnerable to cyber risks that can cripple critical networks, infrastructure and our economy.

speaker: Mr Neil Parekh Nimil Rajnikant (Nominated Member)
text: Such threats often transcend national borders and sectors.

speaker: Mr Neil Parekh Nimil Rajnikant (Nominated Member)
text: The interconnected nature of our modern world also means that a cyberattack in one area can quickly spread and escalate, causing widespread disruption and damage.

speaker: Mr Neil Parekh Nimil Rajnikant (Nominated Member)
text: As the digital landscape evolves, so does the battlefield.

speaker: Mr Neil Parekh Nimil Rajnikant (Nominated Member)
text: The future of defence is no longer confined to traditional domains such as land, air, or sea; it now extends into the digital realm of cyberspace.

speaker: Mr Neil Parekh Nimil Rajnikant (Nominated Member)
text: In response to the increasing complexity of cyber threats, a growing number of militaries have established dedicated cyber units.

speaker: Mr Neil Parekh Nimil Rajnikant (Nominated Member)
text: I was heartened that the Digital and Intelligence Service (DIS) was established as the fourth service of the SAF in October 2022.

speaker: Mr Neil Parekh Nimil Rajnikant (Nominated Member)
text: Notwithstanding, cyber defence is multifaceted, making it impossible for any single entity to tackle alone.

speaker: Mr Neil Parekh Nimil Rajnikant (Nominated Member)
text: Effective cyber defence requires a collaborative approach, one that leverages the collective expertise and resources of various stakeholders, in both public and private sectors.

speaker: Mr Neil Parekh Nimil Rajnikant (Nominated Member)
text: It is essential for the DIS to work closely with other agencies, sharing information, strategies and technologies to build a robust and resilient defence against cyber threats.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair
text: Chairman, one of the topics I have raised over the years in the COS debate has been the use of unmanned systems in warfare.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair
text: One of the perennial problems SAF faces is falling cohort sizes because of falling birthrates.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair
text: This is a trend that is set to continue.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair
text: Against this backdrop, unmanned systems provide a unique opportunity to be able to project force with less manpower.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair
text: For militaries, unmanned technologies can potentially improve operational efficiency through automating repetitive or high-risk tasks, such as using autonomous ground robots for battlefield surveillance or remotely-controlled robots to conduct dangerous bomb defusals.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair
text: More recently, I understand that AI simulators could allow soldiers to conduct drills multiple times in different variations within a short period of time, improving their learning and practice using the least amount of resources.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair
text: As unmanned technologies improve, we are also starting to see platforms that can also execute operations with greater precision and reliability.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair
text: Some of us may know about the DJI, whose flagship drone, the DJI Matrice 350 RTK, is capable of surveying, mapping and doing infrastructure inspection with great precision.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair
text: Other unmanned platforms can navigate challenging terrains and support complex logistical operations with minimal human intervention and supervision.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair
text: Conversely, unmanned platforms from potential aggressors, including non-state actors, also pose a new threat.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Kebun Baru)
text: Chairman, the war in Ukraine has amply demonstrated that drones have fundamentally changed modern warfighting, with tactics surrounding drone deployment and countermeasures evolving rapidly every few months.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Kebun Baru)
text: Drones are now used for reconnaissance, precision strikes and even larger-scale swarm attacks, making them a key factor in asymmetrical warfare.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Kebun Baru)
text: Reports show that militaries worldwide are ramping up their drone operation industries, with the capacity to make and maintain drones in the thousands, if not millions.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Kebun Baru)
text: Given the rapid pace of technology advancements, ongoing conflicts have shown the urgency of staying ahead in drone defence strategies.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Kebun Baru)
text: It is a challenge to develop and operate counter-drone defence systems that are cost-effective against these low-level, low-cost targets.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: Chairman, we are witnessing the rapid rise of emerging and disruptive technologies from AI and quantum computing to advanced robotics and cyber warfare.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: These innovations hold immense potential, but also pose significant challenges, especially when it comes to military security.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: Emerging technologies are not just reshaping industries, they are changing the ways wars are fought.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: We now face the reality of adversaries using AI-driven drones, autonomous systems and cyberattacks to disrupt critical infrastructure, communication and defence mechanisms.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: Take, for example, the use of AI-enabled drones by various state and non-state actors.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: These drones are becoming an increasingly common weapon on the battlefield.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: Ultimately, it is clear that staying ahead of disruptive technology will require not only technological innovation but also strategic foresight and adaptability.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: Our ability to manage, control and protect against these technologies will define the future of warfare and how we defend Singapore.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: Mr Chairman, rigorous and realistic training for our SAF is of utmost importance.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: As General Norman Schwarzkopf once said, “The more you sweat in peace, the less you bleed in war.” Therefore, excellence in training is our first and best line of defence.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: The SAF has long conducted overseas exercises in diverse terrains, climates and environments – critical experiences that are not feasible within our limited land area.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: These large-scale and high-end trainings help our Servicemen keep pace with evolving threats.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: Modern conflicts increasingly involve dense urban settings and hybrid tactics, requiring our soldiers to be adaptable, quick-thinking and responsive to rapidly changing situations.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: Urban warfare, as we have seen in recent conflicts, present unique challenges: the interplay of skyscrapers and subterranean complexes, the constant presence of civilians and the ever-present risk of unconventional tactics.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: No single strategy can be applied to every city block or building.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: Our Servicemen must not only master their equipment but also develop the mental acuity to seize opportunities amid complex situations.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: To that end, the Ministry of Defence has taken proactive steps to enhance urban training.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: These capabilities embody the spirit of continuous improvement for our military, ensuring that every lesson learnt on the training ground translates into greater operational effectiveness.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: Going forward, Mr Chairman, I would like to seek an update from the Ministry on how it intends to build upon these developments.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: Specifically, how will MINDEF continue to refine our training methodology, both overseas and here at home, so that our troops remain primed for the demands of ever more complex battlegrounds?

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: Our collective security hinges on our ability to innovate, adapt and prepare.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: After all, if we embrace challenging training today, we can better safeguard ourselves and our people for tomorrow.

speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang)
text: Chairman, the Minister had shared in the past about the network of international partnerships that MINDEF has established to enable training overseas.

speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang)
text: Such opportunities on foreign land afford the SAF access to precious training space.

speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang)
text: We appreciate these arrangements deeply, given our own very limited land, air and sea space.

speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang)
text: Still, it is just as important that SAF continues to train locally.

speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang)
text: For one, the COVID-19 pandemic taught us that access to overseas training spaces can be cut off quite suddenly.

speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang)
text: More importantly, our soldiers need to train realistically and be familiar with our own physical terrain and context in order to be effective when the need to defend Singapore arises.

speaker: Mr Chong Kee Hiong (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Mr Chairman, finding land available for training is a major challenge for many militaries, especially for a small and densely populated country like Singapore.

speaker: Mr Chong Kee Hiong (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: As we all know, effective military training requires large and open spaces for high-end live firing exercises and large-scale manoeuvres.

speaker: Mr Chong Kee Hiong (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: I was glad to hear about the SAFTI City development from the Minister for Defence last year, especially on how SAF is doing more with less to enhance training experiences for our Servicemen, in spite of our limited land availability.

speaker: Mr Chong Kee Hiong (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Training locally is important so that SAF is familiar with our terrain to be proficient in urban operations.

speaker: Mr Chong Kee Hiong (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: It is also equally important to train overseas for the exposure and experience to build our military forces’ ability to adapt to a wide range of unfamiliar conditions.

speaker: Mr Chong Kee Hiong (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: They need training under a variety of different situations and terrains to enhance their resilience and abilities.

speaker: Mr Chong Kee Hiong (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: This is how we ensure that we have a well-rounded and prepared fighting force.

speaker: Mr Chong Kee Hiong (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: SAF has also been training abroad for many years and we are very appreciative to our foreign partners for the opportunities.

speaker: Mr Chong Kee Hiong (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: I am sure my Parliamentary colleagues would agree that the importance of training both locally and overseas cannot be overstated, as each offers unique benefits that contribute to the overall effectiveness and adaptability of SAF.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: Almost every day, the residents of Sengkang GRC are forced to pause what they are doing as military jets scream past overhead.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: What is worse, the location of the town, close to the northeastern edge of the island, means that they must endure the noise for an extended period as the planes circle round again after making a U-turn to avoid entry into Malaysian airspace.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: Such disturbances are especially disruptive, given how an increasingly larger number of Singaporeans now work from home, at least part of the time.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: Over the years, I and my Parliamentary colleagues have implored RSAF to consider various alternatives to their overflights, to cluster take-offs more, to consider alternative flight paths, to take breaks in the early mornings or during exam periods, and to respect quiet hours.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: In the meantime, however, our residents continue to experience disruptions to their daily activities.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: This advance in aerospace technology offers potentially quieter jet engines with minimal reductions in performance.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: Other technologies, like micro vortex generators, acoustic liners and other types of modifications to engine nozzles, also appear to hold promise.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: In an earlier Parliamentary Question response, Minister Ng Eng Hen indicated that RSAF will continue to monitor such technologies.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: Will the Ministry be able to provide an update on its monitoring efforts?

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: Are there any plans to devote a budget toward researching and incorporating noise reduction technologies into military aircraft here?

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: While I understand that defensive capability and safety considerations should always remain priorities for the Armed Forces, surely the impact that achieving such capabilities have on the daily life of Singaporeans should matter, too.

speaker: Mr Don Wee (Chua Chu Kang)
text: Mr Chairman, as a small city-state with a tumultuous start, it has been deeply embedded in our national psyche that we cannot count on anyone but ourselves to defend Singapore.

speaker: Mr Don Wee (Chua Chu Kang)
text: This has not been mere rhetoric but a principle that has consistently guided the Government’s approach to defence and national security.

speaker: Mr Don Wee (Chua Chu Kang)
text: The Minister for Defence, Dr Ng, has also regularly reminded Members of this House that defence is a long-term business that requires sustained and consistent investment.

speaker: Mr Don Wee (Chua Chu Kang)
text: By maintaining sustainable and stable defence spending that avoids sharp fluctuations, we have equipped the Singapore Armed Forces (SAF) with cutting-edge technology, highly-trained personnel and the necessary infrastructure to confront a spectrum of threats.

speaker: Mr Don Wee (Chua Chu Kang)
text: As we celebrate SG60 this year and look towards the next phase of nation-building, it is imperative that we consider whether our defence spending is aligned with the challenges of tomorrow.

speaker: Mr Don Wee (Chua Chu Kang)
text: Looking at ongoing developments in the world, it is no longer sufficient for SAF to only be well-versed at tackling traditional threats, neither can we afford to be playing catch up on emerging non-traditional threats.

speaker: Mr Don Wee (Chua Chu Kang)
text: The world is also facing the pervasive and fundamental threat of climate change.

speaker: Mr Don Wee (Chua Chu Kang)
text: This will implicate both the conditions in which SAF is expected to train and operate as well as the challenges that SAF may be called on to tackle, especially as a result of extreme weather such as floods and fires.

speaker: Mr Don Wee (Chua Chu Kang)
text: So, while SAF is certainly not responsible for climate change, it must join in collective action to mitigate its impact for Singapore's future.

speaker: Mr Don Wee (Chua Chu Kang)
text: Our investment in defence must continue to be prudent and forward-looking, ensuring that SAF remains an agile force capable of adapting to the dynamic security environment.

speaker: Mr Don Wee (Chua Chu Kang)
text: In that regard, I would like to seek an update on our projected defence spending for this year.

speaker: Mr Don Wee (Chua Chu Kang)
text: In the area of sustainability, militaries often get a bad reputation as the environmental impact of military operations can be substantial.

speaker: Mr Don Wee (Chua Chu Kang)
text: Also, as militaries often naturally prioritise national security and mission readiness, it would not be uncommon for green practices and sustainability to become an afterthought.

speaker: Mr Don Wee (Chua Chu Kang)
text: MINDEF last provided an update on SAF's efforts on environmental sustainability in 2022.

speaker: Mr Don Wee (Chua Chu Kang)
text: Since then, what else has been done and is MINDEF or SAF on track to fulfil its commitments as part of the Singapore Green Plan 2030?

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry
text: Chairman, many current and future security challenges transcend national borders, requiring collective responses and new capabilities.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry
text: No nation is immune to transboundary threats, like terrorism, maritime piracy, cyberattacks and climate change.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry
text: Singapore, being a highly connected city-state with an open economy, is inherently vulnerable to such transboundary threats.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry
text: Even as we have enjoyed relative peace and prosperity, we must build our capabilities to ensure we have operational expertise in dealing with these threats.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry
text: Furthermore, traditional warfare is changing with new domains of conflict emerging alongside conventional military engagements.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry
text: As these threats evolve, new technologies and capabilities, such as secured satellite communications, AI-driven defence systems, robotics, drones and cutting-edge electronic warfare, are increasingly becoming relevant.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry
text: With geopolitical dynamics shifting and many of these capabilities spreading throughout different geographical regions and private sector players, collaboration is now essential.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry
text: Through regular cornerstone events, such as the Shangri-La Dialogue, Singapore has established itself as a valuable convener for bilateral and multilateral security dialogues.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry
text: I am pleased to see new platforms emerging to discuss modern challenges posed by emerging technologies, such as the Digital Defence Symposium, co-hosted by the ASEAN Defence Ministers' Meeting (ADMM) Cybersecurity and Information Centre of Excellence and the S.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry
text: But apart from dialogue, how can we substantively build partnerships to address common security challenges?

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry
text: In particular, given Singapore's limited manpower and resources, we have to be deliberate and identify niches where our expertise can make a valuable impact.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry
text: In this context, how is MINDEF/SAF working with defence partners to address transnational security challenges?

speaker: Miss Rachel Ong (West Coast)
text: Chairman, given the rapid geopolitical shifts and growing security challenges, maintaining strong defence relations is vital for national security, stability and peace.

speaker: Miss Rachel Ong (West Coast)
text: For small nations like Singapore, our security and prosperity are closely tied to navigating international complexities through defence diplomacy.

speaker: Miss Rachel Ong (West Coast)
text: Our approach to defence relations is based on the understanding that no country can tackle transnational threats, such as terrorism, cyberattacks or climate change, alone.

speaker: Miss Rachel Ong (West Coast)
text: In counter-terrorism, Singapore has closely collaborated with regional partners to share intelligence and expertise against the growing terrorism threat.

speaker: Miss Rachel Ong (West Coast)
text: This collaboration has been vital in countering threats from groups, like ISIS, whose activities extend into Southeast Asia.

speaker: Miss Rachel Ong (West Coast)
text: Singapore's involvement has helped prevent attacks in the region and ensured our citizens' safety.

speaker: Miss Rachel Ong (West Coast)
text: Beyond counter-terrorism, Singapore has built strong defence ties with countries, like the US and Australia, to address emerging security challenges.

speaker: Miss Rachel Ong (West Coast)
text: We have consistently worked to build a broad network of defence partnerships with like-minded countries to address these issues collectively.

speaker: Miss Rachel Ong (West Coast)
text: These partnerships strengthen Singapore's position as a reliable international partner, advance our interests and ensure our voices are heard globally.

speaker: Miss Rachel Ong (West Coast)
text: In the face of shifting global power dynamics and emerging security challenges, it is crucial for Singapore to continuously adapt and strengthen these relationships to preserve regional peace and security and safeguard the well-being of our citizens.

speaker: Miss Rachel Ong (West Coast)
text: In this context, I would like to request an update from MINDEF on the current state of Singapore's defence relations with key partners, particularly in strengthening cooperation and building strategic partnerships.

speaker: Miss Rachel Ong (West Coast)
text: How are we advancing our defence diplomacy efforts to address regional security challenges, especially in counter-terrorism and information sharing?

speaker: Miss Rachel Ong (West Coast)
text: What measures are being taken to further deepen these partnerships for Singapore's long-term security?

speaker: Mr Shawn Huang Wei Zhong
text: Mr Chairman, as a small nation, Singapore is vulnerable to external influences and pressures.

speaker: Mr Shawn Huang Wei Zhong
text: Strong diplomatic and defence relations help to mitigate these risks.

speaker: Mr Shawn Huang Wei Zhong
text: Building good relations with our neighbours is particularly important, not solely because of our geographical proximity, but also to enable close working relationships to uphold shared security interests.

speaker: Mr Shawn Huang Wei Zhong
text: With Malaysia, we have strong people-to-people ties, with many crossing the borders to visit family, work and study.

speaker: Mr Shawn Huang Wei Zhong
text: We also work closely on various important fronts, including trade, defence and environmental issues.

speaker: Mr Shawn Huang Wei Zhong
text: With Indonesia, Singapore maintains a multifaceted partnership, engaging in extensive economic cooperation and addressing cross-boundary challenges, like haze.

speaker: Mr Shawn Huang Wei Zhong
text: Much of Singapore's continued survival and prosperity also hinges on a stable, regional environment.

speaker: Mr Shawn Huang Wei Zhong
text: Association of Southeast Asian Nations (ASEAN) is an important platform for Singapore to work with countries with common interests to promote regional stability and to contribute meaningfully to their larger international agenda.

speaker: Mr Shawn Huang Wei Zhong
text: Given the importance of forging strong ties with our neighbours and maintaining ASEAN centrality, what are some of the recent cooperation efforts Singapore has with our regional neighbours as well as with ASEAN?

speaker: Mr Chong Kee Hiong
text: Mr Chairman, Singapore's birth rate has been on a downward trend for years, similar to the situation in many other developed nations.

speaker: Mr Chong Kee Hiong
text: While this is not news, it is important that we continue with our endeavour to address the implications for our national defence.

speaker: Mr Chong Kee Hiong
text: It is a major challenge to maintain a robust defence force with a smaller pool of young Singaporeans eligible for military service.

speaker: Mr Chong Kee Hiong
text: In addition, as our population ages, the proportion of those of prime age that can continue to be part of the reservist pool also decreases.

speaker: Mr Chong Kee Hiong
text: Given the unpredictable state of global affairs, we must be on our guard against potential conflicts or wars.

speaker: Mr Chong Kee Hiong
text: Apart from the countries directly involved, there will be impact on many other countries indirectly, as we have observed from the Russian-Ukrainian War and Israel-Hamas conflict.

speaker: Mr Chong Kee Hiong
text: Our people have always been our greatest asset for national defence.

speaker: Mr Chong Kee Hiong
text: SAF should explore innovative solutions and policies to ensure that we can continue to tap on our key resource pool to maximise their potential.

speaker: Mr Chong Kee Hiong
text: It is in this context that I request MINDEF to share more about how SAF is optimising the deployment of our National Servicemen (NSmen) given our declining cohorts.

speaker: Mr Chong Kee Hiong
text: For example, will SAF tap on technology or even medical advances to augment the capabilities, health or stamina of each NSman?

speaker: Mr Mohd Fahmi Aliman (Marine Parade)
text: Chairman, the binary classification of our servicemen either as combat-fit or non combat-fit has been used by SAF for a long time and has great implications on the vocation options and National Service (NS) experiences available to our servicemen.

speaker: Mr Mohd Fahmi Aliman (Marine Parade)
text: I fully agree that medical exclusions that used to determine deployments may no longer be so relevant in today's operational context, especially with the changing nature of modern warfare and the new digital domains in which our soldiers are expected to operate.

speaker: Mr Mohd Fahmi Aliman (Marine Parade)
text: So, can MINDEF share any updates on this initiative?

speaker: Mr Mohd Fahmi Aliman (Marine Parade)
text: As a conscript armed force, our pre-enlistees come from a diverse range of educational pathways, with different skillsets and individual career interests.

speaker: Mr Mohd Fahmi Aliman (Marine Parade)
text: I am glad to see that MINDEF/SAF recognises this and has been offering multiple schemes that allow students with different educational backgrounds to pursue further qualifications while serving NS.

speaker: Mr Shawn Huang Wei Zhong
text: Mr Chairman, as our population grows increasingly well educated and skilled, our NSmen can also bring to the table a diverse range of talents and experiences that could be useful to SAF.

speaker: Mr Shawn Huang Wei Zhong
text: The NS system should have the necessary structures and processes in place to ensure that we are making the best use of our NSmen's expertise.

speaker: Mr Shawn Huang Wei Zhong
text: This will become increasingly important as Singapore's falling fertility rate affects the number of enlistees the SAF could take in each year.

speaker: Mr Shawn Huang Wei Zhong
text: I believe that this is a good initiative to deploy NSmen to roles that are aligned with the expertise that they have acquired in school or at their workplaces.

speaker: Mr Shawn Huang Wei Zhong
text: We have a win-win situation here as it not only enhances the SAF's operational effectiveness by tapping on specialised skills and expertise, but it also provides NSmen with the opportunity to practise and hone their skills.

speaker: Mr Shawn Huang Wei Zhong
text: This will hopefully give them an increased sense of purpose and fulfilment towards NS as they apply their skills to make a meaningful impact with minimal training required.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Chairman, we face increasing uncertainty and complexity in our security landscape.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Potential threats to our national security include conflicts in our region, acts of terrorism, organised crime and natural disasters.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Our servicemen have to respond to a wide range of emergencies and threat scenarios, such as military attacks or cyberattacks, hostile acts involving explosives, chemical or biological weapons, and more.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: This is particularly challenging for our NSmen because they are not soldiers by profession.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Yet, they must be adequately equipped, both in terms of skills and equipment, to perform their roles effectively and safely.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: To perform any job well, hands-on or real-life exposure is needed for the practice and experience.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: All the more so for our soldiers, who have to perform under a diverse set of high-stakes and time-critical situations that can range from peacetime responses to wartime contingencies.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (Pioneer)
text: All Singaporean sons go through a rite of passage of two years of NS, which is then typically followed by a 10-year training cycle.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (Pioneer)
text: It is a commitment that comes at both a personal and societal cost.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (Pioneer)
text: At the same time, I think I speak for most, if not all, Singaporeans that NS remains necessary for Singapore's defence.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (Pioneer)
text: This is particularly so in today's climate of evolving threats and uncertainties.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (Pioneer)
text: In that regard, there is the responsibility to ensure that the safety of our Singaporean sons is always the top priority.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (Pioneer)
text: As we adapt to new technologies, tactics and environments, it is equally essential that our training safety procedures evolve accordingly.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (Pioneer)
text: I recall attending some high-risk training in the SAF years ago, and these days we have urban warfare and lots of close quarter battle, and chemical, biological, radiological and explosives (CBRE), and overseas exercises exposure such as Exercise Wallaby.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (Pioneer)
text: I would thus like to seek an update from MINDEF on our training safety protocols.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim
text: Chairman the demands of modern warfare continued to evolve.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim
text: So, too must be the tools we use to train our servicemen.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim
text: One of the most exciting areas of innovation in the military today is the integration of advanced technologies aimed at improving training efficacy and ensuring the safety of our troops.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim
text: Technologies like virtual reality (VR) and augmented reality (AR) are revolutionising a how we prepare soldiers for the battlefield.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim
text: They help to develop critical decision-making skills, refine tactics and practice responses in combat situations without physical danger.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim
text: Data from wearable technologies is also invaluable too in safety aspects, preventing heat strokes and over exertion, allowing commanders to intervene before a situation escalates.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim
text: AI-driven systems can be used to identify areas for improvement.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim
text: By incorporating these cutting-edge technologies, the military is not only improving the quality of training but also ensuring that our servicemen are better prepared, safer and more resilient in the face of increasingly complex and dangerous challenges.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Chairman, mental health is as important as our physical health.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: The need for the maintenance and enhancement of mental health with any needed diagnosis and treatments is still in the process of gaining wider recognition amongst our people.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Nonetheless, we have been making strides as a nation in terms of advancing mental health care awareness and access.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: What was once surrounded by stigma and kept in the shadows has in recent times been acknowledged as important as physical health.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: This change was perpetuated by the global pandemic over the past few years, which forced many of us to confront the mental strain of isolation, uncertainty and stress.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: In the context of the military, soldiers are trained to be resilient, strong and disciplined.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: We usually think of the military as a sector where strength is defined by physical power, endurance, or the ability to push through pain, but mental toughness is just as critical as physical strength.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: We now understand that mental health challenges, stress, anxiety, or the pressure of adapting to new environments are a natural part of life and can affect anyone regardless of their background, age or rank, particularly for many of our young men who enlist at the age of 18, the stress of gruelling physical training, the mental load from adjusting to military life, and the emotional struggles of being away from their loved ones and the comforts of home can be overwhelming for them.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: In particular, how can we better facilitate our Singaporean sons transition to NS and set them up for a successful training stint?

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: Our soldiers face operational stress, regimentation, and the challenges of balancing military life.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: Ensuring they are psychologically resilient is essential for their well-being and operational readiness.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: Could MINDEF provide an update on recent efforts to strengthen the mental resilience of our soldiers?

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: How are resilience-building strategies incorporated into training to help our soldiers better manage stress and pressure?

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: Beyond counselling services, are there plans to enhance peer support networks or introduce structured mental wellness programmes within SAF units?

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: Could technology also play a role in providing early mental health interventions?

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan (Mountbatten)
text: They want to be able to plan for their studies or plan whether they can take on a temporary job, pending their NS.

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan (Mountbatten)
text: Since its release, have there been any enhancements made to the OneNS Portal?

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan (Mountbatten)
text: Will the One NS web portal be able to provide such information to students who are enlisting soon.

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan (Mountbatten)
text: Can NSmen use the portal to apply for deferment of their NS training?

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan (Mountbatten)
text: Has there been any survey among NSmen or to assess the effectiveness and usefulness of the portal?

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan (Mountbatten)
text: I hope that MINDEF recognises that in this digital age, continuous updates are necessary to keep up with user needs and improve user experience.

speaker: Ms See Jinli Jean (Nominated Member)
text: At its COS last year, MINDEF shared that a one-stop Central Manpower Base (CMPB) would be developed at Bukit Gombak to serve the needs of servicemen and their families, as well as the public living in the area.

speaker: Ms See Jinli Jean (Nominated Member)
text: I understand that servicemen can tap on the regional health hub for comprehensive primary and specialist healthcare as well as health screening services.

speaker: Ms See Jinli Jean (Nominated Member)
text: First, could MINDEF provide an update on the consolidation of medical services at this regional health hub within the new CMPB?

speaker: Ms See Jinli Jean (Nominated Member)
text: Second, apart from services for servicemen, could MINDEF provide details on the amenities which would be open to the public?

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: Chairman, NS is indispensable to Singapore, given our unique challenges as a small nation with no natural resources.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: The invasion of Ukraine and the current challenges it is still facing, has further underscored the importance of a strong defence.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: It is through NS that we maintain the peace and security we enjoy today, ensuring that our nation is prepared, capable, and ready to defend our sovereignty when necessary.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: At its core, the strength of our defence lies in our people.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: What has MINDEF done to continue to inspire our servicemen in its important mission?

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: What has MINDEF done over the past year to recognise and appreciate the efforts of our servicemen?

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: Additionally, family support plays a vital role in the success of NS.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: Families provide emotional stability and strength, helping servicemen navigate the challenges of their NS journey.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: Facilities like SAFRA offer recreational, social, and educational activities for NSmen and their families, fostering a supportive environment and giving them a sense of belonging to the bigger NS family.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: As we move forward, are there further improvements or enhancements that Singaporeans can look forward to in SAFRA facilities for our servicemen and their families?

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: Mr Chairman, national defence is the primary goal of NS, but NS should also be an investment in human capital.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: MINDEF should transform NS into a value of creative experience for our NSmen by ensuring appropriate remuneration, relevant training and stronger education and career integration.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: First, full time NSmen's pay should reflect their contributions to national defence.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: The argument that duty and employment are mutually exclusive is flawed.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: SAF regulars are paid market salaries while serving the same national defence mission.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: NSFs make personal sacrifices, delaying their education and career, and consequently, sometimes even marriage and children, because of NS.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: Pay that acknowledges these realities will strengthen their commitment to national defence.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: This way, NS can serve as a launchpad for future opportunities rather than an educational and career detour.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam
text: Chairman, NS has long been the bedrock of our nation's defence – an institution through which generations of Singaporean sons and daughters have stepped forward to protect our homeland.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam
text: The contributions of our full-time NSmen and women are invaluable.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam
text: At the same time, we recognise that these commitments may impact their educational and career trajectories.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam
text: A recent 2023 Institute of Policy Studies report on public attitudes towards NS found broad support for conscription, yet highlighted concerns that time spent in service could affect subsequent transitions to study or to employment.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam
text: One key recommendation was for MINDEF to strengthen support for service-men-and-women during their final months of NS, helping them prepare for the next phase of life.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam
text: This move of course reflects the Ministry's commitment to investing in our servicemen's development, both during and after their time in uniform.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam
text: Chairman, with these developments in mind, I would like to request an update on the concrete measures that MINDEF has implemented, or plans to implement, to facilitate our Servicemen’s smooth transition into their next chapter, be it as students or in the workforce.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam
text: Specifically, I seek more details on how MINDEF’s initiatives, such as SkillsFuture@NS, will continue to equip our full-time NSmen with the skills, knowledge and confidence to excel in their post-NS endeavours.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Mr Chairman, besides conventional military threats, there are many other threats and risks that could disrupt our daily life and threaten our way of life in Singapore.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Even though five years have passed, we must not forget how quickly the COVID-19 pandemic disrupted our daily lives and every sector of our society.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Our peace and stability can be fragile and should not be taken for granted.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: In addition, intense ongoing conflicts and geopolitical tensions persist, not just in far-flung regions but close to home as well.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Conflicts far abroad may still cause Singapore to be vulnerable to shocks, such as supply chain disruptions, economic instability and widening socio-political divisions.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Have there been any findings or analysis on the resilience gaps in our society?

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: It is difficult to predict what the next black swan event that could destabilise Singapore might be, but we must do our best to prepare Singaporeans and build resilience.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: How relevant is the role of Total Defence in raising the level of civic preparedness among Singaporeans for disruptions to daily life?

speaker: Mr Alex Yam
text: Chairman, the inaugural Exercise SG Ready was a timely demonstration of how crises and disruptions can strain our daily lives – from power and water outages to digital connectivity failures, widespread cyberattacks, disinformation campaigns and drone threats.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam
text: These simulations challenged our readiness across multiple fronts, ensuring that Singaporeans remain prepared to respond swiftly and effectively to such hybrid threats.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam
text: We have witnessed how these dangers can escalate in real-world contexts.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam
text: Amidst the still ongoing Russia-Ukraine conflict, repeated strikes on Ukraine’s energy infrastructure have led to prolonged power blackouts.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam
text: As part of our SG60 commemorations, the exercise invited Singaporeans to reflect on the crises and disruptions we have overcome over the six decades of our Independence and to brace ourselves for potential future threats.

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan
text: I served my NS many years ago and have always been convinced of the importance of NS and the need for all Singaporeans to understand that only we are responsible for defending our nation.

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan
text: We cannot depend on any other nation to help us deal with an aggressor country.

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan
text: Last week’s incident in the White House is a grim reminder to all nations of the need to be self-sufficient.

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan
text: In recent years, as we observed the wars in other countries and how some nations have rallied to respond in the face of aggressive forces.

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan
text: The nations that have responded best tend to be the ones with higher levels of social resilience.

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan
text: Social resilience is important and is crucial because it helps communities withstand, adapt to and recover from crises that could impact social cohesion.

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan
text: To build social resilience, we have to foster a society that embraces staying together and staying strong even when under stress.

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan
text: Singaporeans must learn to adapt to new challenges and be ready to contribute to developing solutions to tackle them head-on.

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan
text: This requires community networks and support systems to help people share resources and provide support to one another during times of crises.

speaker: Miss Rachel Ong
text: As we see in conflicts around the world, a nation’s strength and ability to defend itself rely on the collective power of its people.

speaker: Miss Rachel Ong
text: Our youths play a critical role in ensuring a secure and resilient future.

speaker: Miss Rachel Ong
text: Investing in youth participation in Total Defence is an investment in national stability.

speaker: Miss Rachel Ong
text: When young people take ownership of national resilience, they inspire others and foster a culture of preparedness that endures for generations.

speaker: Mr Chong Kee Hiong
text: Mr Chairman, Total Defence is the cornerstone of Singapore’s national security strategy.

speaker: Mr Chong Kee Hiong
text: Total Defence is premised on the understanding that our security, stability and prosperity depend on the collective commitment and efforts of all Singaporeans and sectors of our country.

speaker: Mr Chong Kee Hiong
text: Each of us has a part to play to defend Singapore.

speaker: Mr Chong Kee Hiong
text: We are facing complex security threats and challenges even during peacetime, from terrorism and cyberattacks, to pandemics and climate change.

speaker: Mr Chong Kee Hiong
text: We must build our resilience as a people.

speaker: Mr Chong Kee Hiong
text: We need to be prepared through exercises and drills to cope with the potential disruptions from emergencies and crises.

speaker: Mr Chong Kee Hiong
text: We commemorated 40 years of Total Defence last year.

speaker: Miss Rachel Ong
text: Chairman, the Advisory Council on Community Relations in Defence (ACCORD) has long served as a vital bridge between Singapore’s defence sector and the broader community.

speaker: Miss Rachel Ong
text: It plays a critical role in garnering public support for our defence efforts, building trust and fostering understanding across various societal segments.

speaker: Miss Rachel Ong
text: Through ACCORD, we have seen active engagement with diverse groups, including ethnic communities, businesses and grassroots organisations.

speaker: Miss Rachel Ong
text: These efforts have not only heightened public awareness of our national defence needs but also encouraged active participation in Total Defence, ensuring every Singaporean understands their role in safeguarding our nation.

speaker: Miss Rachel Ong
text: How has ACCORD further strengthened its outreach and engagement with the community?

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal
text: These museums must remain engaging and relevant for future generations as security threats evolve.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal
text: How is MINDEF leveraging these museums to deepen public understanding of Total Defence, especially beyond military security, such as digital threats and social resilience?

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal
text: Are there efforts to modernise exhibits by incorporating interactive elements, simulations or digital storytelling to enhance learning experiences?

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal
text: Beyond education, these museums can foster stronger connections between the public and MINDEF.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal
text: Could MINDEF explore initiatives, such as using soldiers for guided tours, to incorporate real-life experiences into the learning process?

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal
text: As Singapore continues to evolve, how will MINDEF ensure that these museums remain dynamic, relevant and impactful in shaping our national defence consciousness?

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh
text: Chairman, Total Defence is a collective effort, and it would be useful to tap on our people’s ideas and feedback to obtain fresh and a wide range of perspectives on how we can defend Singapore.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh
text: By empowering the public to contribute meaningfully to our nation’s security and stability, Singaporeans will feel a deep sense of belonging and build stronger community networks.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh
text: We should provide flexibility to allow ground-up initiatives to experiment with methods and solutions that may not be immediately feasible in large-scale Government programmes.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh
text: Let us consider crowdsourcing of innovative ideas from the broader community, particularly from youths who have fresh perspectives and savvy skills.

speaker: The Minister for Defence (Dr Ng Eng Hen)
text: Mr Chairman, that we are living in turbulent times is plainly evident.

speaker: The Minister for Defence (Dr Ng Eng Hen)
text: Some of my colleagues who have filed their cuts said so in so many words.

speaker: The Minister for Defence (Dr Ng Eng Hen)
text: Mr Vikram Nair said that the collective security and the rules-based world order appeared to be fraying.

speaker: The Minister for Defence (Dr Ng Eng Hen)
text: Mr Desmond Choo said the world is now a far more dangerous and uncertain place.

speaker: The Minister for Defence (Dr Ng Eng Hen)
text: Mr Shawn Huang said the war in Ukraine highlights the vulnerability of smaller states to larger powers and how we need to be prepared.

speaker: The Minister for Defence (Dr Ng Eng Hen)
text: So, how do we prepare Singapore and our people for a disruptive future, even a disrupted one?

speaker: The Minister for Defence (Dr Ng Eng Hen)
text: For leaders everywhere, that surely must be the overriding concern as the global order changes before our very eyes.

speaker: The Minister for Defence (Dr Ng Eng Hen)
text: It has happened before, not only for Singapore, but the entire ASEAN region and beyond, where your basic assumptions change precipitously and your futures are altered rapidly.

speaker: The Minister for Defence (Dr Ng Eng Hen)
text: How do we prepare Singaporeans for this kind of change?

speaker: The Minister for Defence (Dr Ng Eng Hen)
text: We want to learn from history, surely, about how the world might change when big power diplomacy dominates.

speaker: The Minister for Defence (Dr Ng Eng Hen)
text: And we ask, as we look at these examples, how are the fates of nations decided when big power politics and big power diplomacy dominate in this literal world order?

speaker: The Minister for Defence (Dr Ng Eng Hen)
text: It is decided in the corridors of power and then declared publicly as a fait accompli.

speaker: The Minister for Defence (Dr Ng Eng Hen)
text: If the powers that be had decided differently, we could very well have been under Dutch rule and a radically different future from today.

speaker: The Minister for Defence (Dr Ng Eng Hen)
text: Just as a lark, I typed into your ChatGPT and asked what would happen to Singapore if we were under Dutch rule?

speaker: The Minister for Defence (Dr Ng Eng Hen)
text: It gives you a very, very good answer.

speaker: The Minister for Defence (Dr Ng Eng Hen)
text: Well, it will tell you that a lot of things will change.

speaker: The Minister for Defence (Dr Ng Eng Hen)
text: Or change can be inflicted through open aggression and brute force.

speaker: The Minister for Defence (Dr Ng Eng Hen)
text: I do not like this situation, I am going to deal with you.

speaker: The Minister for Defence (Dr Ng Eng Hen)
text: Whether you like it or not, whether you can withstand it or not.

speaker: The Minister for Defence (Dr Ng Eng Hen)
text: And barely two months later, the hitherto impregnable "Gibraltar of the East", as we were referred to, fell, and Japanese occupation ensued in Singapore.

speaker: The Minister for Defence (Dr Ng Eng Hen)
text: I have been to the Pearl Harbor museum twice.

speaker: The Minister for Defence (Dr Ng Eng Hen)
text: It is fascinating every time I go there.

speaker: The Minister for Defence (Dr Ng Eng Hen)
text: They lay it out in wonderfully chronological order.

speaker: The Minister for Defence (Dr Ng Eng Hen)
text: There are actually two halls, one before the attack, one after.

speaker: The Minister for Defence (Dr Ng Eng Hen)
text: In retrospect, it is so logical that these countries would do what they did.

speaker: The Minister for Defence (Dr Ng Eng Hen)
text: You see the Japanese ambassador to the US writing his letter to Franklin D Roosevelt, and you understand why countries behaved as they did.

speaker: The Minister for Defence (Dr Ng Eng Hen)
text: But the Pearl Harbor attack, that day in infamy, caught the US and Allied powers, even with their vast intelligence network, by surprise.

speaker: The Minister for Defence (Dr Ng Eng Hen)
text: If you look at the military strategy of the Pearl Harbor attack – I come from MINDEF, so, I have some inkling of what military plans are – the Japanese Pearl Harbor attack, an audacious pincer attack.

speaker: The Minister for Defence (Dr Ng Eng Hen)
text: We sit here and we watch the events.

speaker: The Minister for Defence (Dr Ng Eng Hen)
text: Many Members of Parliament (MPs) have expressed how every week, there are different headlines, something that you have never see.

speaker: The Minister for Defence (Dr Ng Eng Hen)
text: No one can predict the future precisely, but the feel of change is in the air.

speaker: The Minister for Defence (Dr Ng Eng Hen)
text: Seasoned columnists who have witnessed historically churning events liken our time to that before the First World War and ask if we are sleepwalking into our future.

speaker: The Minister for Defence (Dr Ng Eng Hen)
text: In the aftermath of World War I, four empires, some which had existed for hundreds of years, laid waste.

speaker: The Minister for Defence (Dr Ng Eng Hen)
text: It changed the map of the world – of borders, of alliances, of ethnic groups, of societies en masse.

speaker: The Minister for Defence (Dr Ng Eng Hen)
text: For Europe, especially after the recent NATO meetings and the Munich Security Conference (MSC) – I was there, so I could feel the mood directly – there is presently great consternation.

speaker: The Minister for Defence (Dr Ng Eng Hen)
text: The Associated Press said, "NATO is in disarray." This was after the US announced that its security priorities lie elsewhere.

speaker: The Minister for Defence (Dr Ng Eng Hen)
text: The Wall Street Journal, "Planned US-Russia talks over Ukraine throw Europe into crisis." More dramatically, Politico asked, "Is this the end of NATO?" The trans-Atlantic partnership has remained strong for more than a century despite great stresses, not least two World Wars.

speaker: The Minister for Defence (Dr Ng Eng Hen)
text: Only time will tell if these headlines and fears are accurate or over-reactions.

speaker: The Minister for Defence (Dr Ng Eng Hen)
text: More pointedly, what is in store for Asia?

speaker: The Minister for Defence (Dr Ng Eng Hen)
text: That, to me, is the quintessential question for our time.

speaker: The Minister for Defence (Dr Ng Eng Hen)
text: That, to me, is the most important thing that we have to decide.

speaker: The Minister for Defence (Dr Ng Eng Hen)
text: Your residents on the ground will ask you, as MPs, what is in store?

speaker: The Minister for Defence (Dr Ng Eng Hen)
text: I know that this is our Budget and our COS.

speaker: The Minister for Defence (Dr Ng Eng Hen)
text: We also know that this is an election year.

speaker: The Minister for Defence (Dr Ng Eng Hen)
text: But the answer to that question is going to occupy us for at least a decade.

speaker: The Minister for Defence (Dr Ng Eng Hen)
text: It is going to decide the fate of Singapore and Singaporeans for this generation.

speaker: The Minister for Defence (Dr Ng Eng Hen)
text: All the headlines that you read – it is not business as usual.

speaker: The Minister for Defence (Dr Ng Eng Hen)
text: It is a political earthquake, with a tsunami coming.

speaker: The Minister for Defence (Dr Ng Eng Hen)
text: We do not know when the tsunami will occur.

speaker: The Minister for Defence (Dr Ng Eng Hen)
text: We know that it registers on the political Richter scale.

speaker: The Minister for Defence (Dr Ng Eng Hen)
text: You know something is coming, you do not know how to predict it accurately, when, in what shape and form.

speaker: The Minister for Defence (Dr Ng Eng Hen)
text: But whatever comes, whatever comes, we must face our future resolutely.

speaker: The Minister for Defence (Dr Ng Eng Hen)
text: Singapore has thrived since our Independence because we took the world as it is and not what we wished it to be.

speaker: The Minister for Defence (Dr Ng Eng Hen)
text: We responded to daunting challenges as one nation, with grit, perseverance, sacrifice and hard realism.

speaker: The Minister for Defence (Dr Ng Eng Hen)
text: We must now do the same as we enter into uncharted waters.

speaker: The Minister for Defence (Dr Ng Eng Hen)
text: Before 1965, we were not in charge of our own fate.

speaker: The Minister for Defence (Dr Ng Eng Hen)
text: So, we could have blamed other countries – the British or other large powers.

speaker: The Minister for Defence (Dr Ng Eng Hen)
text: But now, as an independent and sovereign nation, we Singaporeans have agency and can decide and do all we can to secure our future together.

speaker: The Minister for Defence (Dr Ng Eng Hen)
text: And certainly, building our own defences to protect our own interests must take priority.

speaker: The Minister for Defence (Dr Ng Eng Hen)
text: We count on no one else to protect Singapore, but ourselves.

speaker: The Minister for Defence (Dr Ng Eng Hen)
text: Because ultimately, it has to be a strong SAF.

speaker: The Minister for Defence (Dr Ng Eng Hen)
text: We are not a threat to anyone and wish all to be friends.

speaker: The Minister for Defence (Dr Ng Eng Hen)
text: But as the saying goes, strong fences – and I would add, defences – make good neighbours.

speaker: The Minister for Defence (Dr Ng Eng Hen)
text: Mr Desmond Choo and Mr Shawn Huang pointed out the progress of the SAF.

speaker: The Minister for Defence (Dr Ng Eng Hen)
text: It is now a modern four Service military able to operate effectively across all domains of air, land, sea and digital, as Mr Neil Parekh also alluded to.

speaker: The Minister for Defence (Dr Ng Eng Hen)
text: But building capacity and capability for the SAF is a continual exercise.

speaker: The Minister for Defence (Dr Ng Eng Hen)
text: In the interest of time, I will first name the big-ticket items, starting with conventional capabilities that some of you have asked for.

speaker: The Minister for Defence (Dr Ng Eng Hen)
text: That programme is on track, with all four custom-made submarines for the Republic of Singapore Navy (RSN).

speaker: The Minister for Defence (Dr Ng Eng Hen)
text: It is the first time we have had custom-made.

speaker: The Minister for Defence (Dr Ng Eng Hen)
text: I do not know whether you refer to those submarines as second-hand or third-hand, but anyway, they were not custom-made for us.

speaker: The Minister for Defence (Dr Ng Eng Hen)
text: This is the first time that we custom-made them.

speaker: The Minister for Defence (Dr Ng Eng Hen)
text: They will be operational, all of them, by around 2028.

speaker: The Minister for Defence (Dr Ng Eng Hen)
text: These submarines were manufactured in the icy waters there.

speaker: The Minister for Defence (Dr Ng Eng Hen)
text: I remember when then-Prime Minister Lee launched two submarines.

speaker: The Minister for Defence (Dr Ng Eng Hen)
text: They had to bring out blankets and warmers for those of us on land.

speaker: The Minister for Defence (Dr Ng Eng Hen)
text: Two submarines have returned, are already plying our tropical waters and they are functioning well in our conditions.

speaker: The Minister for Defence (Dr Ng Eng Hen)
text: But four submarines are not optimal for a fleet.

speaker: The Minister for Defence (Dr Ng Eng Hen)
text: Submarines are subjected to more rigorous and frequent maintenance cycles, stringent checks as you can imagine, because they need to operate under intense pressure, literally.

speaker: The Minister for Defence (Dr Ng Eng Hen)
text: This is why most navies that operate submarines have more than four – Australia, Indonesia, Vietnam, to name a few of our close neighbours.

speaker: The Minister for Defence (Dr Ng Eng Hen)
text: They are going to replace our Victory-class corvettes, which have been around since 1989.

speaker: The Minister for Defence (Dr Ng Eng Hen)
text: So, calculate for yourself – nearly 35 years old.

speaker: The Minister for Defence (Dr Ng Eng Hen)
text: The MRCVs are larger and have greater range than the Victory-class corvettes – about three times further.

speaker: The Minister for Defence (Dr Ng Eng Hen)
text: The MRCV is actually not one ship but a mothership with unmanned platforms.

speaker: The Minister for Defence (Dr Ng Eng Hen)
text: Some of you have spoken about unmanned platforms.

speaker: The Minister for Defence (Dr Ng Eng Hen)
text: Together with its suite of advanced sensors and combat systems, the MRCVs will strengthen our Navy's ability to safeguard our maritime interests.

speaker: The Minister for Defence (Dr Ng Eng Hen)
text: Our Fokker 50 maritime patrol aircraft are also due for replacement.

speaker: The Minister for Defence (Dr Ng Eng Hen)
text: Our Fokkers have served with distinction for three decades since 1993.

speaker: The Minister for Defence (Dr Ng Eng Hen)
text: The RSAF is now looking intently and evaluating appropriate replacements.

speaker: The Minister for Defence (Dr Ng Eng Hen)
text: Two possible ones: the Boeing P-8A and Airbus C295.

speaker: The Minister for Defence (Dr Ng Eng Hen)
text: We have recently confirmed the purchase of these F-35As from the US and look forward to the establishment of our F-35 and F-16 fighter detachment at Ebbing Air National Guard Base.

speaker: The Minister for Defence (Dr Ng Eng Hen)
text: It is not just that we buy the planes from the US, not that they acquiesce to us training in the US.

speaker: The Minister for Defence (Dr Ng Eng Hen)
text: These moves reflect the strength of our defence relationship with the US and the continued commitment to a multi-decade partnership.

speaker: The Minister for Defence (Dr Ng Eng Hen)
text: For the Army, we will have a new infantry fighting vehicle (IFV).

speaker: The Minister for Defence (Dr Ng Eng Hen)
text: So, I have finished the sea, the air, let us move on to the Army.

speaker: The Minister for Defence (Dr Ng Eng Hen)
text: The new infantry fighting vehicle, I think most of the MPs who were still serving SAF are from the Army here.

speaker: The Minister for Defence (Dr Ng Eng Hen)
text: It will also be equipped with counter-Unmanned Aerial System capabilities.

speaker: The Minister for Defence (Dr Ng Eng Hen)
text: The Army's High Mobility Artillery Rocket System (HIMARS) – I think many of you would have read about it during the Russia-Ukrainian War.

speaker: The Minister for Defence (Dr Ng Eng Hen)
text: These were quite useful and effective – they, too, will be upgraded with more capable rockets.

speaker: The Minister for Defence (Dr Ng Eng Hen)
text: With these added large-ticket items for air, land and sea, the SAF as a relatively small military would have been transformed into a state-of-the-art military with platforms comparable to advanced militaries elsewhere and fit for our security purposes.

speaker: The Minister for Defence (Dr Ng Eng Hen)
text: But as some MPs would have alluded to, there is a common dictum, a cautionary caveat, that militaries must be careful that they do not arm themselves to "fight the last war".

speaker: The Minister for Defence (Dr Ng Eng Hen)
text: I take all your points, I accept them.

speaker: The Minister for Defence (Dr Ng Eng Hen)
text: There have been new developments that are going to impact the way militaries conduct their operations.

speaker: The Minister for Defence (Dr Ng Eng Hen)
text: So, for the past decade, indeed, that is what we have been doing.

speaker: The Minister for Defence (Dr Ng Eng Hen)
text: When you ask yourself, how do you respond to these new changes?

speaker: The Minister for Defence (Dr Ng Eng Hen)
text: For the militaries, it boils down to two things: structure and platforms.

speaker: The Minister for Defence (Dr Ng Eng Hen)
text: If you do not have both, then you are not really serious about re-organising and meeting these demands.

speaker: The Minister for Defence (Dr Ng Eng Hen)
text: If you have not changed your structure, if you have not gotten new capabilities and platforms, then you have not been adequately responding.

speaker: The Minister for Defence (Dr Ng Eng Hen)
text: We need to reorganise the SAF, to equip it, to incorporate emerging technologies and capabilities.

speaker: The Minister for Defence (Dr Ng Eng Hen)
text: Mr Vikram Nair and Mr Neil Parekh referred to this in terms of the DIS.

speaker: The Minister for Defence (Dr Ng Eng Hen)
text: I am glad that it reaffirms the confidence that was formed about the SAF.

speaker: The Minister for Defence (Dr Ng Eng Hen)
text: Remember I said unless you have structure and a new platform, you really are not adapting.

speaker: The Minister for Defence (Dr Ng Eng Hen)
text: The fact that we can stand up two new commands reflects progress.

speaker: The Minister for Defence (Dr Ng Eng Hen)
text: It will have two centres: the Digital Ops-Tech Centre and the SAF Artificial Intelligence (AI) Centre.

speaker: The Minister for Defence (Dr Ng Eng Hen)
text: The mission for these new commands and centres is to bring to bear for the SAF the full effects of new digital hardware and software.

speaker: The Minister for Defence (Dr Ng Eng Hen)
text: In the prosecution of missions now, or previously, we will use mainly conventional capabilities.

speaker: The Minister for Defence (Dr Ng Eng Hen)
text: Yes, you would enhance it with software aspects, but in modern military affairs, the comparative advantage is how you meld the two and bring to effect the capabilities of both.

speaker: The Minister for Defence (Dr Ng Eng Hen)
text: That is the job of the new commands and centres.

speaker: The Minister for Defence (Dr Ng Eng Hen)
text: The new command will have to deal with hostile digital threats against Singapore from state and non-state actors.

speaker: The Minister for Defence (Dr Ng Eng Hen)
text: Because as you can imagine, if anyone attacks our digital backbone, our essential services will be crippled.

speaker: The Minister for Defence (Dr Ng Eng Hen)
text: And it is obvious that as a small geographic entity, we are vulnerable.

speaker: The Minister for Defence (Dr Ng Eng Hen)
text: It will impact economic and social well-being and will have a direct impact even on our security forces – the SAF and the Home Team – because we have to operate in this country.

speaker: The Minister for Defence (Dr Ng Eng Hen)
text: We have redundancies but we have to protect our digital backbone.

speaker: The Minister for Defence (Dr Ng Eng Hen)
text: And that mission to deal with such external actors falls on the new command.

speaker: The Minister for Defence (Dr Ng Eng Hen)
text: Mr Henry Kwek and Mr Vikram Nair asked about unmanned platforms.

speaker: The Minister for Defence (Dr Ng Eng Hen)
text: I am glad they did because this is something that we are doing serious work and intense work on reorganisation in all the Services.

speaker: The Minister for Defence (Dr Ng Eng Hen)
text: Because militaries must not only be able to integrate that new technology and force structure and operations, but counter and defend against these threats.

speaker: The Minister for Defence (Dr Ng Eng Hen)
text: As some of you rightly alluded to, it is proven that drones will be part of modern warfare.

speaker: The Minister for Defence (Dr Ng Eng Hen)
text: It is only how much and whether you are prepared.

speaker: The Minister for Defence (Dr Ng Eng Hen)
text: And they are not producing it because they are under intense pressure; they know how useful it is.

speaker: The Minister for Defence (Dr Ng Eng Hen)
text: Drones have been used to target support, gather intelligence, strike operations, decoy, relay signals and many other functions.

speaker: The Minister for Defence (Dr Ng Eng Hen)
text: And, in fact, the SAF has already progressed in the use of unmanned platforms.

speaker: The Minister for Defence (Dr Ng Eng Hen)
text: So, for example, in the Singapore Straits, the Unmanned Surface Vessels (USVs) conduct patrols now and these USVs – if you happen to be on a boat along the Singapore Straits, you can say hello to them – they are equipped with electro-optic devices, radars and a 12.7-millimetre weapon system.

speaker: The Minister for Defence (Dr Ng Eng Hen)
text: They use lights, sirens, long-range acoustics device, and where justified, they can fire shots with their remote gun system.

speaker: The Minister for Defence (Dr Ng Eng Hen)
text: Unmanned Aerial Vehicles (UAVs) are now becoming part and parcel of the soldier’s arsenal in the Army, very much like how scouts use binoculars and can tap in and with far greater range and precision.

speaker: The Minister for Defence (Dr Ng Eng Hen)
text: And so, commanders can tap into a common picture from these various drones, inputs from the unmanned platforms to fight more effectively and smarter.

speaker: The Minister for Defence (Dr Ng Eng Hen)
text: But it is in the Air Force that the pace and scale of drones have grown exponentially.

speaker: The Minister for Defence (Dr Ng Eng Hen)
text: So much so, that the Air Force has found it necessary to reorganise and to establish a new UAS Warfare and Tactics Centre.

speaker: The Minister for Defence (Dr Ng Eng Hen)
text: This new centre will drive the development of UAS warfare and its integration with the other forces and working with industries and tech agencies.

speaker: The Minister for Defence (Dr Ng Eng Hen)
text: If we can leverage on drones as platforms, on the flip side, the SAF will also need to build up its capabilities to defend against UASs.

speaker: The Minister for Defence (Dr Ng Eng Hen)
text: And in these small commercial UASs are easily procured on the open market, I think, Mr Vikram Nair alluded to it.

speaker: The Minister for Defence (Dr Ng Eng Hen)
text: I do not want to give the wrong impression that it is so easy and that there are comprehensive solutions to deal with all UASs.

speaker: The Minister for Defence (Dr Ng Eng Hen)
text: That would be a wrong impression and would not be telling you the honest truth.

speaker: The Minister for Defence (Dr Ng Eng Hen)
text: Small drones are, in fact, hard to detect.

speaker: The Minister for Defence (Dr Ng Eng Hen)
